summary: A booklet of step-by-step scenarios for trying out ARPANET host computers. Using annotated scripts from the MIT-DMCG PDP-10 system, it shows logging in, using simple features, getting online help and chatting with other users, to help newcomers and system programmers.

plainLanguage.summary: This booklet shows example sessions on ARPANET host computers. It explains what a user types, what the host replies, and what each step does.

questions: how did people log in to arpanet hosts in 1971
what is the arpanet scenario booklet
subtitle: Annotated sample sessions for logging in to and trying ARPANET host computers.

tldr.problem: A newcomer needed practical guidance for logging in to different ARPANET hosts, each with its own commands and terminal conventions.
tldr.mechanism: The booklet presents annotated scripts showing user input, host responses, and brief explanations for login, help, messaging, file work, and other tasks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 254 is a guide to specific host systems and services in 1971, not a protocol specification.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 254 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. Its commands describe particular host systems as presented in the 1971 booklet.

sections.title: Purpose of the Scenarios
sections.content:
RFC 254 is a scenario booklet intended to help people sample ARPANET host computers. The examples cover login, simple facilities, online help, communication with other users, and, where suitable, editing and running a small program.

The scripts assume the MIT-DMCG PDP-10 environment, but the author says they can be adapted for use from other systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Each scenario is a guided practice session on a host computer. The examples are meant to help newcomers get started with remote systems.

sections.title: How to Read a Script
sections.content:
Comments appear in parentheses, and user input is marked with underlining in the printed booklet. A carriage return is shown as <CR>; a blank represents a space. A backslash marks escape to the local user TELNET in the assumed MIT-DMCG environment.

The table of contents lists host computers and their Network addresses, including sites where no scenario was available.
sections.plainLanguage: Formatting helps separate what the person types from what the host says. Notes beside the lines explain the purpose of each action.

sections.title: Tasks Shown in the Sessions
sections.content:
The examples include connecting to hosts, logging in, reading or sending messages, checking who is using a system, and using online help. Some sessions show editing, compiling, and running a small program; others demonstrate a TELNET connection from one host onward to another.

Several listed hosts had no usable login or were not providing service when the booklet was prepared, so the RFC gives no complete scenario for them.
sections.plainLanguage: The scripts demonstrate ordinary tasks such as messaging, finding help, and running a program. They also record when a listed host could not be tried.
